coastline-sprint.intro: Build every rule before connecting it to graphics: course, fresh drivers, traffic, movement, results and pad mapping.

parts.title: Course units and a reusable clamp
parts.why: length and checkpoint distances use arbitrary road units; limit and bonus use seconds. clamp confines a value to a closed interval, which is useful for speed, nitro and steering position. curve uses normalized course progress to keep the opening straight and soften the final bends; hill combines two waves so elevation is not a single repetitive slope. These are sampled functions, not meshes.
parts.try: Change limit from 65 to 10 and restart. You should lose sooner, while the road length and checkpoint positions remain unchanged; then restore 65.

parts.title: Create independent drivers
parts.why: Each call returns a new mutable object. x is across the road, z is progress along it, and speed is road units per second. elapsed measures the result time while time counts down. index selects controls and car colour. Nitro, checkpoint and collision timers belong to each player, preventing P2 activity from draining P1 resources.
parts.try: Start split play and compare both timers/nitro displays. Accelerate only P2; P1 progress should stay independent.

parts.title: Seed opponents without updating them twice
parts.why: The factory creates 24 fresh traffic records with alternating lanes and a small set of speeds. updateDriver exits for a driver whose result is final, caps an unusually long frame, advances the two clocks and decays cooldowns toward zero. The app will move traffic once per frame, outside the per-player loop.
parts.try: Restart twice and confirm traffic returns to its opening positions. Duplicating the traffic update inside each viewport would make split-screen traffic twice as fast.

parts.title: Integrate speed and steering in seconds
parts.why: boost is a condition, not a stored second timer. Nitro drains while boosting and refills otherwise, with clamp keeping it between zero and one. Speed integrates throttle, braking and coasting drag using dt. The lateral expression combines player steering with outward curve drift. The off-road branch subtracts speed and clamps to zero, so grass cannot accelerate a stationary car.
parts.try: Change the coasting term 500 to 1000. Release throttle on a straight and observe faster deceleration, then restore it.

parts.title: Throttle repeated sound and collision responses
parts.why: This continues the if condition opened immediately above. Skid requires speed and hard turning/braking or an off-road position; its timer prevents a sound on every frame. Progress then advances by speed times dt. Collision uses independent forward and lateral distance thresholds. The 1.4-second cooldown stops one overlapping traffic car from registering dozens of impacts.
parts.try: Drive into traffic and watch HITS. It should increase once, not once per rendered frame. Reducing the cooldown is an intentional difficulty change, not a rendering change.

parts.title: Consume checkpoints and finish once
parts.why: The checkpoint condition continues the preceding if. The index points to the next unclaimed checkpoint; incrementing it is what prevents repeated time bonuses. Reaching the course end clamps progress and sets finished; only otherwise can the zero-time branch set lost. Returning event names keeps audio outside these rules.
parts.try: Pass one checkpoint slowly. The bonus should be awarded once even though you remain beyond its distance on later frames.

parts.title: Translate hardware into game intent
parts.why: Optional chaining makes a missing pad safe. The helper reads analog values for triggers/buttons, applies a dead zone to the stick, and returns the same steer/accel/brake/boost shape as keyboard input. Math.max allows either a trigger or a face button to request throttle. The simulation therefore does not need a special gamepad movement path.
parts.try: Gently move the stick near centre. Small noise should be ignored; a larger motion should steer continuously. Hardware mappings still need checking on your controller.

coastline-sprint.intro: Turn the simulation into a pseudo-3D picture, including every projection, sprite and HUD step.

parts.title: Paint a background in viewport coordinates
parts.why: The renderer receives w and h instead of reading the full canvas size, so the same function works in a half-height view. Background layers overwrite the viewport every frame. A sine ridge gives a cheap skyline; its tiny progress-dependent phase makes the horizon react as you travel. None of these pixels changes the road collision rules.
parts.try: Temporarily change the sky colour. Both split-screen views should change without affecting handling.

parts.title: Project many road samples
parts.why: SEG is longitudinal spacing and road is half-width in world-like units. dx accumulates curvature and x accumulates that change again, bending the road smoothly across depth. The reciprocal scale makes far samples smaller. The projected centre subtracts player lateral position, while projected height compares the local hill with the distant hill. Each point stores enough information for road and roadside objects to agree.
parts.try: Change 180 samples to 90. The visible horizon distance shrinks; this does not shorten the course.

parts.title: Join neighbouring samples into strips
parts.why: A quad connects two projected cross-sections. ratio widens or narrows the same geometry for shoulders, asphalt and lane paint. The loop runs far to near so closer strips cover distant ones. It skips folded/offscreen sections, alternates stripe colours by world distance, and makes thin lane quads by copying points with smaller widths.
parts.try: Reverse the loop on a temporary copy and look for near/far overlap errors. Restore the far-to-near order before continuing.

parts.title: Crop one sprite cell and anchor its feet
parts.why: drawImage receives a source rectangle followed by a destination rectangle. Modulo selects the sheet column, integer division selects its row, and fw/fh are cell dimensions. The destination subtracts half width and full height so cx/cy is the object base, not its top-left. Rounding and disabling smoothing preserve the supplied pixel art.
parts.try: Choose a different player frame temporarily. The car should change pose without shifting the road or changing collision size.

parts.title: Depth-sort scenery and traffic
parts.why: Roadside records are generated around the current travel segment. Traffic and the other player join the same visible-object list only when ahead and inside the draw distance. Sorting by descending z paints distant sprites first. Matching each object to a road sample gives consistent curve, hill, lane offset and apparent size. The other player is a visible rival, not another traffic collision body.
parts.try: Watch a traffic car near a hill while approaching. It should grow and follow the same projected road rather than sliding independently across the sky.

parts.title: Finish with a local car and a data-driven HUD
parts.why: The player car is drawn last in a fixed screen location; steering chooses its sprite cell. Width responds to viewport height, which keeps the split view usable. HUD text reads state rather than calculating it again. Result overlays test finished/lost and show elapsed time or TIME UP; they do not end the race themselves.
parts.try: Resize the browser and compare solo/split HUDs. Restart from a result and confirm the overlay disappears when fresh driver state is created.

coastline-sprint.intro: Wire the whole racer together: a tiny page frame, the UI file, resources, intent, state changes, simulation loop and independent viewports.

parts.title: Imports and a minimal page frame
parts.why: Imports give the host access to rules, renderer, audio, the UI runtime and file paths. mount receives the HTML-tier root. The only markup built in code is a shell and a 16:9 canvas, made with createElement and a few style properties; every menu, button and line of text now lives in ui/menu.ui.json instead of a giant HTML string. Padding above and below the canvas leaves room for the UI bar and notice line.
parts.try: Change the shell padding top from 56px to 100px and reload. The canvas moves down, the UI bar stays anchored to the top of the shell; restore the value afterwards.

parts.title: Load the UI file and keep handles
parts.why: createUI(shell).load fetches ui/menu.ui.json, builds it into an isolated shadow root over the shell and returns a screen. menu.$('name') returns a node handle by the name you gave it in the Designer and throws a clear error if the name is missing. Handles are kept in constants so the game loop never searches the DOM; setting text or visible later touches only that node.
parts.try: Open ui/menu.ui.json in the UI Designer, rename the node 'overlay' to 'intro', save, reload Play and read the Console: menu.$('overlay') should now throw a message naming the missing node. Rename it back.

parts.title: Canvas context, images and shared state
parts.why: The 2D context, audio object and key set are created once. The image loader resolves only on load and rejects with the missing path on error, and await ensures both sheets exist before drawView receives them. Run variables then hold players, shared traffic, mode, menu/result state and the previous frame timestamp; pad and keyboard translate browser state into rule inputs.
parts.try: Temporarily misspell a sprite filename, reopen Play and inspect the Console. Restore it; a missing resource should fail clearly instead of producing a silent empty car.

parts.title: Reset one complete race from a button
parts.why: starting blocks overlapping asynchronous audio setup. Split mode first verifies a connected controller; no half-initialized second player is created when it is absent. New drivers and traffic replace old run state, held keys are cleared, and canvas focus returns to play. Audio activation stays inside this click path so the browser can authorize playback. finally releases the starting guard even if audio fails.
parts.try: Restart while holding a key, then release it. Fresh state and key clearing should prevent the old run from continuing invisibly.

parts.title: Pause logic and wire controls
parts.why: The guard excludes menu/results. A disconnected P2 pad prevents unsafe resume. Pause updates state, overlay, sound context and keys together. The following button assignments connect page intent to these functions; mute changes the label from the helper result, and track change requests music only after a context exists.
parts.try: Pause during a race and switch tracks. Resume and confirm the timer did not advance while paused.

parts.title: React to named UI actions
parts.why: Each button in the UI file has an action name such as one, two, pause or restart. menu.on(action, fn) subscribes to that name, so the code never needs element IDs or querySelector. The select emits track when its choice changes, and the mute handler writes the new label back through the node's text property. Moving a button or restyling it in the Designer cannot break any of this.
parts.try: In the Designer change the Restart button's action from restart to again and save without touching app.js. Pressing the button now does nothing until you also change menu.on('restart') to menu.on('again'); then undo both.

parts.title: Maintain held keys instead of moving in key events
parts.why: keydown/keyup update the Set; movement will read it once per simulation frame. preventDefault stops arrows/Space scrolling the page only while playing. P ignores auto-repeat. Blur clears held inputs and pauses, avoiding stuck steering when focus changes. These window listeners live for this mounted page, which Nord replaces when Play is reopened.
parts.try: Hold steering, move focus away, return and resume. The car must not remain stuck turning after the key was released outside the page.

parts.title: Advance the world once, then report results
parts.why: requestAnimationFrame supplies milliseconds; dividing by 1000 converts to the rules’ seconds. The cap avoids a giant step after a stalled frame. Disconnection can pause both views before simulation. Shared traffic moves once, each driver advances with its own input, and returned events trigger sounds. The whole race reaches result only when every driver has finished or lost.
parts.try: In split mode let one timer expire first. The other driver should still be able to finish while the finished view displays its result.

parts.title: Render two cameras without duplicating simulation
parts.why: Engine rate/gain follows P1 speed. Each viewport saves canvas state, clips its own rectangle and translates the origin before calling drawView. restore prevents the second view inheriting the first view’s clip/translation. The separator is drawn once, notices reflect current pad/audio state, and scheduling the next frame keeps the loop alive even while paused so UI can still respond.
parts.try: Remove restore only on a temporary copy and observe the broken second view; put it back. The getter object at the end is for inspection/tests, not another game loop.

coastline-sprint.intro: Describe the whole menu as data: layout containers, buttons, a select, text with placeholders and the intro card. The UI Designer edits this file.

parts.title: Theme variables and the transparent root
parts.why: The file starts with a version and a name, then theme variables: bg, panel, border, fg and accent override the engine defaults for this screen only. The root is a full-size panel whose style removes the default background, border and padding, so it acts as an invisible layer above the canvas while its children are positioned by anchors.
parts.try: Change the accent colour from #304a61 to #aa3355 and reload. All buttons change colour at once because they share the variable; restore the old value.

parts.title: A row of buttons with action names
parts.why: An hbox lays its children out in a row with a gap and padding, anchored to the top edge at full width. Each button names an action under on.pressed; the game subscribes to those names with menu.on. The select lists its options and reports changes as the track action. Layout and wording are therefore editable without touching code.
parts.try: Drag the Restart row above Pause in the Designer's tree and save. The order on screen changes, while the game still responds to every button.

parts.title: Notice line and the intro card
parts.why: The notice label shows the template text {notice}; the game fills it with menu.set('notice', ...) and only changed values touch the page. The overlay is a centred vertical box with a translucent card style. Its title and body labels use rich text: [b] for bold and [br] for line breaks, parsed safely into spans rather than injected as HTML.
parts.try: Change the title text to [color=#ff8866]COASTLINE[/color] SPRINT, save and reload to see rich text colour part of the heading.

coastline-sprint.intro: Build the complete local-audio helper: activation, cached decoding, voices, crossfade and cleanup.

parts.title: Own resources for one run
parts.why: The constructor records configuration separately from browser audio objects. A Map caches a promise for each path, and a Set tracks live voices. Keeping these on the instance gives one owner for cleanup and makes repeated effects reuse decoded audio. The AudioContext is deferred until a user gesture because browser playback permission belongs to that gesture.
parts.try: Start a fresh page and inspect the helper before clicking Start: it has configuration but no running AudioContext.

parts.title: Decode each path once
parts.why: The first load stores the entire asynchronous fetch/decode operation in the Map. A second request receives that same promise even if downloading is still in progress. Checking response.ok turns a missing file into a meaningful error instead of attempting to decode an HTML error page. decodeAudioData produces a reusable buffer, not a playing sound.
parts.try: Temporarily mistype one SFX path. Trigger it and observe the visible audio problem; restore the path and reopen Play to clear the rejected cached request.

parts.title: Turn a buffer into a voice
parts.why: A BufferSource is single-use: the cached buffer can be reused, but each playback needs a new source. A GainNode gives that voice its own volume before reaching the master. Loop/rate options handle music and engine pitch. The non-looping voice cap bounds overlapping effects; onended disconnects nodes and removes the finished voice from the Set. Errors become an inspectable problem rather than stopping gameplay.
parts.try: Lower the voice volume for one event. Its loudness should change without affecting music or changing the file itself.

parts.title: Keep game events independent of file paths
parts.why: play looks up a symbolic name in config.sfx, so collision code can request crash without knowing where the recording lives. music creates a looping voice, fades its gain in, fades the old voice out and schedules the old source to stop. Capturing the old song lets both overlap briefly rather than cutting abruptly.
parts.try: Switch between the two supplied music tracks while playing. Listen for the overlap; do not put music() inside the animation loop.

parts.title: Pause and dispose the right owner
parts.why: Mute changes the master gain, leaving individual volume relationships intact. Suspend/resume controls the AudioContext clock alongside a paused game. Dispose closes the whole context and clears voice ownership. This is distinct from caching a buffer: cached data may exist while no voice is playing.
parts.try: Mute, unmute, pause and resume. Then restart the scene/app and verify there is one soundtrack rather than another copy layered over the old one.

coastline-sprint.intro: Choose recordings through data rather than hardcoded paths in gameplay.

parts.title: Keep symbolic sound names stable
parts.why: music is an ordered list used by the track selector. sfx maps event names returned by updateDriver to local files. Changing a path replaces a recording without editing physics or rendering; changing a key would require changing event producers too. Both music tracks and every referenced effect are included in the download.
parts.try: Replace only crash with your own short recording, keeping the key crash. Reopen Play and collide with traffic to hear the replacement.

coastline-sprint.intro: Read the complete Nord page entry point and its failure path.

parts.title: Load the local runtime and start the app
parts.why: The document declares encoding and viewport, creates the mount container and loads local code. The module imports mount from app.js and awaits initialization for the HTML-tier root. The ready/error flags are inspection signals used by browser checks; they are not a second simulation. The catch logs and exposes initialization errors. The page is served over HTTP so local module and asset URLs resolve consistently.
parts.try: Temporarily rename the imported main module on a copy and reopen Play. Inspect the Console/error path, then restore the correct name.

coastline-sprint.intro: Read every project field that tells Nord which host, display and services to use.

parts.title: Identify the project and choose its presentation
parts.why: format and engineVersion identify the serialized contract, while name/id give human and stable application identity. type chooses the host; startScene is used by a scene backend and is empty for these HTML apps. Display fields request dimensions, fit behaviour, pixel-art treatment and background. Physics selects a runtime engine; the rail shooter uses custom rules with none, while HTML-hosted libraries are initialized in their own modules.
parts.try: Change only the display title/name in a copy and reopen the project. Do not change the stable ID casually if you want to keep the same save namespace.

parts.title: Distinguish scene actions from HTML event handling
parts.why: The input object maps action names to keyboard codes for Nord scene scripts. Vector Patrol reads these through this.input. HTML-tier hosts in the other projects read their own DOM events, so editing this action table alone does not rewrite those handlers. plugins/ui declare ordinary scene services and skin/theme; any remaining desktop configuration is the native capability contract rather than a browser CORS override.
parts.try: For Vector Patrol, add a second fire key and test it. For an HTML app, locate its key handler instead of expecting this table to change DOM input.

coastline-sprint.intro: Read the supplied sprite sidecar used by Nord’s asset tools.

parts.title: Describe cell geometry and asset identity
parts.why: type declares a spritesheet, frameWidth/frameHeight specify each cell and nearest filtering preserves pixel edges. anims is empty because this racer picks static directional cells itself. Tags organize the asset in tools. The renderer’s explicit crop dimensions must agree with these cell dimensions; metadata is not an automatic steering animation.
parts.try: Compare frame sizes with sprite() calls in render.js. Replace a sheet only after preserving that cell contract or updating both sides.

coastline-sprint.intro: Read the supplied sprite sidecar used by Nord’s asset tools.

parts.title: Describe cell geometry and asset identity
parts.why: type declares a spritesheet, frameWidth/frameHeight specify each cell and nearest filtering preserves pixel edges. anims is empty because this racer picks static directional cells itself. Tags organize the asset in tools. The renderer’s explicit crop dimensions must agree with these cell dimensions; metadata is not an automatic steering animation.
parts.try: Compare frame sizes with sprite() calls in render.js. Replace a sheet only after preserving that cell contract or updating both sides.

vector-patrol.intro: Read the complete rail-shooter simulation, including every timer, collision, spawn and end condition.

parts.title: Give a run one state object
parts.why: newFlight creates fresh arrays and scalar fields for a run. time controls encounters; distance scrolls scenery; x/y describe the fighter’s corridor position. fire/spawn/gate/cell are countdowns, while bossHP and bossZ describe the later encounter. won/lost stop future ticks. None of this requires a browser or a mesh, so the same state can be exercised by small rule tests.
parts.try: List which fields are timers and which are coordinates. Change only hp to 50, reopen Play and confirm the HUD starts at half hull.

parts.title: Read one intent and advance clocks
parts.why: tick exits once a result is final, bounds dt, then integrates travel and clamped steering. Every countdown is updated in the same seconds-based clock. Roll starts only after its cooldown reaches zero, sets a shorter invulnerability window and emits a sound event. Holding fire creates a shot only when its interval expires, so framerate does not determine firing frequency.
parts.try: Double the fire interval from 0.16 to 0.32. Holding Space should produce roughly half as many shots; restore the original value.

parts.title: Spawn waves and rewards on separate schedules
parts.why: An increasing serial ID gives repeatable sine/cosine spawn positions. Enemy spawn delay shrinks as time advances but has a minimum; enemy firing starts with staggered timers. Gates and energy cells use independent countdowns, and ordinary spawns stop before the carrier. Resetting a countdown on spawn is what prevents creating an object on every later frame.
parts.try: Change the first gate countdown in newFlight from 18 to 5. It should arrive earlier without making enemies fire faster.

parts.title: Centralize hull loss and grace
parts.why: Every damage source calls this closure. It ignores hits while shielded or after a result, clamps hp at zero, gives a short grace window and emits crash. Enemy motion and firing are separate: z brings them toward the player, and hostile vx/vy are calculated when a shot is created. Contact consumes the enemy even if the shield prevents damage.
parts.try: Activate roll immediately before contact. The visual roll and the shorter damage shield are related but distinct timers.

parts.title: Introduce the carrier and its fan pattern
parts.why: The encounter is time-driven, while approach distance is clamped to 48 so the carrier remains ahead. bossFire creates five shots with different horizontal velocities. These are ordinary hostile records; the same bullet collision path handles both enemy and carrier fire. That reuse keeps boss code from inventing a second damage system.
parts.try: Change the fan loop limits to -1 and 1 on a copy. You should see three shots per burst; restore five before continuing.

parts.title: Resolve a player shot against one target
parts.why: Shots move forward, then test a depth window and XY distance against living enemies. Setting z to 999 consumes a hit shot, and break prevents the same shot hitting another drone in that loop. Enemy death awards score and explosion once. The carrier check additionally rejects a shot after a player death or prior victory.
parts.try: Lower drone hp to one in the spawn record. A single hit should remove one drone and award 100, without damaging every drone in the array.

parts.title: Make the result exclusive and process hazards
parts.why: The final carrier hit sets won and adds the bonus. Later damage calls see that flag and cannot turn the same winning frame into a death. Hostile bullets advance on their stored velocities and are moved behind the scene after a hit. Gates have a passed flag so their reward/penalty is evaluated once while crossing the player plane.
parts.try: Reach a gate and inspect whether its event occurs once. Temporarily remove passed on a copy to understand why overlap over several frames needs a consumption flag.

parts.title: Consume pickups, prune arrays and enforce the deadline
parts.why: A nearby cell heals with an upper bound, gives score and moves behind the player for removal. filter creates the next living arrays, discarding dead enemies and offscreen shots/gates/cells. These bounds matter because a view pool is finite. The deadline marks a non-winning run lost, then the event list returns to the controller for audio.
parts.try: Watch arrays in the Console during a long run; old objects should disappear. Changing a mesh’s visibility alone would not remove its simulation record.

vector-patrol.intro: Connect all simulation decisions to Nord lifecycle, actions, UI, save data and resource cleanup.

parts.title: Create state and name UI screens
parts.why: Imports separate rules, view and audio. start creates fresh run state and resource owners, loads the best score from Save and creates the persistent flight HUD. Screen names let the controller show/clear one group of labels and buttons without deleting another. Nord calls start after scene entities are available, which is why FlightView can find Fighter and Carrier now.
parts.try: Change the HUD position and reopen Play. It should move without changing the simulated fighter coordinates.

parts.title: Build launch controls and explain actions
parts.why: The menu callbacks capture this controller instance. Launch is a user-gesture entry for audio, while mute changes the audio owner. The instruction label joins separate lines without embedding rules in UI text. Pause and Restart buttons remain on the HUD screen; Restart delegates creation of a fresh scene to Nord.
parts.try: Use Restart before launching and after pausing. The new controller should return to the launch menu with no old labels left behind.

parts.title: Handle input that must work while paused
parts.why: A paused scene does not update, so P is handled by a window listener rather than only inside update. Ignoring repeat prevents rapid toggles from a held key. Blur pauses only an active unfinished run. launch clears the menu and unlocks/starts sound; its started guard prevents duplicate launches. Audio failures become visible state instead of destroying the scene.
parts.try: Hold P down rather than tapping it. It should toggle once. Switch away from the window mid-flight and return to find a paused run.

parts.title: Keep pause UI and the engine in agreement
parts.why: This method changes the controller flag, game pause state, sound context and menu screen as one operation. Ended or unlaunched runs ignore it. Resume clears the temporary pause screen and restarts both clocks. Calling only game.pause without a reachable external resume action would strand the user.
parts.try: Pause and click the same button to resume. Verify the hull/time values stay fixed during the pause.

parts.title: Route actions, sound events and the one-time result
parts.why: The retro action toggles the view. vec creates a directional input, down sustains firing and pressed triggers one roll. tick returns events that select local recordings. The bossMusic flag prevents restarting the carrier song every frame. finished gates the result handler, which writes a new best only on victory and shows one result label. Finally view.draw and draw project the state into meshes and text.
parts.try: Launch, lose and wait several seconds. The loss message should not multiply. Inspect the best-score slot: losing should not overwrite it with a lower score.

parts.title: Format state without changing it, then release resources
parts.why: The HUD method builds readable strings from current state; it does not decrement timers or grant score. onDestroy removes window listeners, releases the view and sound and clears both UI groups. Resuming during teardown prevents an old paused controller from leaving a new scene unable to tick. This cleanup is why scene restart can be safe repeatedly.
parts.try: Restart several times and press P once. One press should cause one toggle, not a toggle from every old controller.

vector-patrol.intro: Follow every conversion from rule records to Nord entities, native pools and retro materials.

parts.title: Keep the backend and imported palette
parts.why: The view stores Babylon’s engine/scene/canvas plus the script’s Nord game. It walks imported meshes and extracts either PBR albedoColor or standard diffuseColor. The colour’s hex string is a Map key, so equal palette colours share one shader material. Originals are retained for teardown rather than destroyed.
parts.try: Select a coloured drone in the scene and compare it in clean/retro mode. A single grey material for every mesh would lose the imported palette.

parts.title: Bind shader attributes and uniforms explicitly
parts.why: ShaderMaterial receives actual source strings and a declared interface. position/normal are vertex data; world/worldViewProjection are matrices; uColor/uRetro/uGrid are custom uniforms. A new colour creates a new material once, while subsequent meshes reuse it. The original material pair is recorded before assignment.
parts.try: Rename a custom uniform only in GLSL on a temporary copy and observe the error or missing effect. Restore both shader and binding names together.

parts.title: Find reusable entities and make simple effect materials
parts.why: Names bridge the authored scene to this view: fourteen drones and three gates already exist. The local material helper creates unlit emissive colours for shots, dots and cells so those tiny objects remain readable. These materials are view resources, not new gameplay records.
parts.try: Rename Drone0 only in the scene on a copy to see why scene names are a contract. Restore it before testing combat.

parts.title: Allocate bounded native pools once
parts.why: pool creates boxes, assigns a shared material and records every mesh for disposal. The four pool sizes reflect different expected object counts. Terrain then gets one lit material and a ground mesh, separate from unlit effects. Allocating here rather than on every shot avoids repeated GPU setup during combat.
parts.try: Compare the 40-shot pool with the maximum shot lifetime and fire interval. If you raise fire rate dramatically, you must reconsider pool capacity too.

parts.title: Add cheap canyon landmarks and a view target
parts.why: Low-tessellation cones become alternating ridges. A hemispheric light illuminates those lit materials and a target points the scene camera into the corridor. Initialization ends by applying retro settings, ensuring resolution and shader toggles begin in the same mode.
parts.try: Reduce the ridge tessellation on a copy. The silhouette changes while collision rules remain exactly the same.

parts.title: Synchronize framebuffer and shader quality
parts.why: Hardware scaling reduces the rendered pixel dimensions relative to the display canvas. CSS imageRendering chooses nearest-style presentation. uRetro selects clean/quantized behaviour, and uGrid derives snapping from the actual render dimensions, not a guessed window size. Reusing this method keeps all materials synchronized when C is pressed.
parts.try: Toggle C while watching a moving model edge. Resolution, vertex steps and colour bands should change together.

parts.title: Place Nord entities from arrays
parts.why: The player’s transform uses state directly; the roll is a visual angle derived from a timer. entities enables only used pooled entities and copies record coordinates. Enemy rotation is visual decoration; it does not move the collision centre. Carrier visibility depends on encounter and win state, so victory removes it without inventing a new simulation condition.
parts.try: Stop firing and watch unused drone slots: they must be disabled rather than left visible at their last position.

parts.title: Place primitive pools and wrap ground motion
parts.why: Native Babylon meshes use setEnabled/position instead of Nord entity properties. The same index-to-record rule draws shots, hostile shots and pickups. Ground dots and ridge positions use modulo distance to recycle a fixed set of meshes, making continuous travel without continuously allocating scenery.
parts.try: Temporarily remove the modulo from ground-dot motion and observe dots leaving permanently; restore it to maintain the repeating corridor.

parts.title: Restore borrowed resources, destroy owned ones
parts.why: Imported meshes belong to scene entities, so the view restores their borrowed materials if they still exist. It destroys materials/meshes/light it created and resets engine scaling for the next scene. This distinction between borrowed and owned resources prevents both leaks and accidental destruction of scene assets.
parts.try: Restart after toggling clean mode. Check the new run initializes consistently and the Console has no disposed-material errors.

vector-patrol.intro: Read both complete GLSL programs; matrix conversion and quantization are small enough to understand line by line.

parts.title: Move from object vertices to a screen grid
parts.why: precision controls floating-point calculation quality. Attributes arrive per vertex; uniforms are shared inputs. The world-view-projection matrix creates clip coordinates. Dividing XY by W gives projected coordinates, which are rounded to a grid and multiplied by W again. mix uses uRetro to select original or snapped positions. The transformed normal is passed to the fragment shader for lighting.
parts.try: Make uGrid smaller in setRetro, then compare a drone edge. Larger visible steps should appear without changing the drone’s simulation position.

parts.title: Light, dither and quantize colour
parts.why: The fragment program normalizes directions and clamps the dot product so back-facing light contributes no negative value. A small base light preserves silhouettes. gl_FragCoord selects one of four ordered dither offsets; quantization rounds each channel to sixteen levels. mix keeps a clean comparison mode and alpha one makes models opaque. This is flat-colour stylization, not texture warping.
parts.try: Set uRetro to zero through the C toggle, then re-enable it. Compare colour bands separately from vertex position changes.

jengatedris.intro: Build every grid rule, from literal shape cells through rotation, hold, gravity and garbage.

parts.title: Define seven pieces as four local cells
parts.why: W/H set board dimensions. Each SHAPES entry lists four offsets in a local four-by-four box, not four positions in the world. A type index selects one entry; colour values use type plus one so zero remains empty. These tables are shared by geometry and previews, preventing a preview shape from disagreeing with collision.
parts.try: Count the offsets in each entry: every piece must have four. Change a colour rather than geometry first, then verify active/preview cells stay consistent.

parts.title: Generate reproducible bags
parts.why: The colour table includes empty and garbage colours. random updates a 32-bit seed and scales it to a fraction. next fills a bag with all seven types, shuffles it using a shrinking index range, then pops one type. Saving the generator in the state makes seeded openings reproducible in tests and battles; it is not a secure random source.
parts.try: Start two newGrid states with the same seed and compare several pieces. They should agree until different operations consume their random streams.

parts.title: Convert local cells and test a candidate
parts.why: cells copies offsets before rotating them so the global SHAPES table stays unchanged. Each quarter-turn maps x/y through the four-cell box, then adds the active piece origin. fits checks all four cells, allowing negative y during entry but rejecting side/bottom collisions and occupied visible cells. spawn resets rotation/fall and checks immediate overflow.
parts.try: Move a piece against a wall. A rejected candidate should not change the original offsets or move another piece of that type.

parts.title: Initialize independent rows and test movement transactionally
parts.why: Array.from creates distinct row arrays. Shared rows made with fill(oneArray) would corrupt multiple rows at once. next is prepared before spawn consumes it. move creates a candidate object, tests it, then commits it; the boolean lets soft drop and gravity decide whether to lock. No pixel coordinates appear in these decisions.
parts.try: Temporarily write one board cell in the Console. Only its own row should change.

parts.title: Try kicks and lock four cells
parts.why: Square rotation is a no-op. Other rotations try horizontal offsets in priority order and accept the first fit; if none fit, state stays unchanged. lock first detects cells above the visible board, then writes type+1. It removes full rows, scores using the old level, computes the next level, prepends fresh empty rows and resets the hold gate before spawning. The goal sets a final result.
parts.try: Create a near-full row in a test copy, clear it, and verify the top row becomes empty and score changes once.

parts.title: Dispatch player intentions and implement hold
parts.why: The dispatcher stops at game over and clears lastClear for this operation. Soft drop either moves and scores or locks; hard drop repeatedly tries move until blocked, scores by distance and locks once. Hold has empty and swap cases. Passing false to spawn during a swap preserves the next queue, and held prevents repeated swaps before lock.
parts.try: Hold twice before locking. The second press should do nothing. After locking, hold should become available again.

parts.title: Separate gravity, garbage and ghost prediction
parts.why: Gravity accumulates seconds until the level-dependent delay passes, then attempts one grid step. Garbage shifts the board upward and adds one row with a seeded hole; occupied cells pushed out or a blocked active piece cause top-out. ghost moves a copy down until the next candidate fails, so it predicts Space without changing the active piece.
parts.try: Compare the ghost with the actual hard-drop landing. In battle, watch garbage push existing rows upward rather than overwrite the bottom row.

jengatedris.intro: Build every piece of the separate real-physics survival mode.

parts.title: Load local physics and make a static container
parts.why: The optional script load uses the packaged Phaser build, whose Matter namespace supplies the solver. The engine gets gravity plus a floor and two static side walls. Static means the solver does not accelerate those bodies under gravity. This coordinate system is canvas pixels and milliseconds, separate from grid cells and seconds.
parts.try: Change gravity from 0.8 to 0.4 temporarily. Pieces should descend more slowly while grid mode stays unchanged.

parts.title: Spawn one compound instead of four loose blocks
parts.why: The state owns every body and the active piece. spawn uses the same SHAPES offsets to make four rectangles, but Body.create combines them into one rigid object with friction, restitution and density. Colour is render data. Resetting time/settle for each spawn gives every active piece its own control window.
parts.try: Rotate a falling piece. Its four cells should stay joined; independent Matter bodies would fall apart.

parts.title: Apply controls, step the solver and detect settling
parts.why: The dt cap limits solver steps. Left/right input contributes force; Q/E changes angular velocity and Down adds a downward force. Engine.update expects milliseconds. A slow body must remain slow for 0.65 seconds after its opening second to count as settled; the seven-second timeout keeps the game progressing. Before spawning, the stack-height check can lose the run, while surviving eighteen pieces wins.
parts.try: Tap rotate, release it and watch contacts change the angle. A simple grid y increment could not produce this motion.

parts.title: Draw actual solver vertices and release the world
parts.why: Matter compounds include a parent part; drawing parts.slice(1) avoids drawing that extra bounding part. Polygon vertices already contain physical rotation and translation, so no separate canvas angle calculation is needed. The returned dispose callback clears bodies and engine state when changing mode.
parts.try: Switch Physics → Grid → Physics. A fresh tower should start, with no old bodies falling into the new world.

jengatedris.intro: Read the entire host page and client loop for all three modes.

parts.title: Create the board and mode controls
parts.why: Imports select rules and optional physics. The mounted page declares mode/restart/pause buttons, a full-size game canvas, status fields, a next/hold preview and local control explanations. IDs are the link to the wiring below. The same canvas renders grid or physics, but each mode keeps its own rules.
parts.try: Find each button ID and its later onclick assignment; no button should rely on its visible text as a program identifier.

parts.title: Describe and collect battle connection details
parts.why: The remaining markup adds player name, room and API address, plus Join/Ready/Leave and an opponent canvas. Inputs are ordinary HTML so typing a room should not move a piece. Footer best-score text is a display target. The next code obtains canvas contexts and a Set for held physics controls, chooses a local default API address and initializes the local run.
parts.try: Click the room input and press A/D. The text should change without shifting the active piece.

parts.title: Implement a request and accept a snapshot

parts.why: Join posts room/name before switching mode, so a failed connection leaves the local game usable. Successful join disposes physics and accepts the authoritative snapshot.
