parts.try: Change one accent colour on a copy and reopen Play; no gameplay or saved-document data should change.

parts.title: Lay out board and previews
parts.why: Flex layout keeps board and sidebar together; canvas rules preserve crisp pixels without changing internal canvas dimensions. Sidebar/label/input rules establish readable configuration controls.
parts.try: Resize slowly and compare CSS display size with the fixed canvas.width used by rendering.

parts.title: Clear auxiliary content and stack on narrow screens
parts.why: The rival float is cleared before footer text. The media query changes the layout direction and page padding for small windows rather than altering grid width or physics coordinates.
parts.try: Narrow below 620 pixels. The sidebar should move below the board while the rules still use ten columns.

nord-office.intro: Build all office rules: map, players, movement, tasks, pranks, pathfinding and shift results.

parts.title: Use readable map and station data
parts.why: Each map string is one row; matching widths keep indexing predictable. Walls/desks are collision tiles, while JOBS supplies the station name, location and puzzle kind. PUZZLES stores a visible faulty JavaScript line, answer choices and the expected index. The three mistakes are off-by-one iteration, assignment versus equality and milliseconds versus seconds. These are data interpreted by rules/UI, not executable snippets from a remote player.
parts.try: Count one map row and move a station on a copy. Keep JOBS coordinates and the corresponding visible marker consistent.

parts.title: Create fresh jobs and players
parts.why: JOBS.map copies definitions into mutable run records, so completing a job does not alter the global station catalogue. owner/work/version are runtime fields. Team score/morale/time/phase belong to the shift; each player owns position, intended direction, active job, prank cooldown and completion count. Names are length-limited at the boundary.
parts.try: Start two fresh state objects and complete a task in one. The other state and the JOBS definitions should remain unchanged.

parts.title: Reset a run without disconnecting the roster
parts.why: The reset changes phase, clocks, score, morale and log, then restores stations and player work. It preserves player IDs/names and the room roster so an online rematch does not require joining again. Incrementing job version changes the next puzzle sequence. This reset is app-specific state replacement, not Nord scene reload.
parts.try: Restart a shared shift. Both human names should remain, while their jobs, scores and positions return to the opening state.

parts.title: Move a small body through a tile grid
parts.why: walkable floors fractional coordinates and treats out-of-map positions as blocked. movePlayer normalizes diagonals before multiplying by speed and seconds. Testing four corner offsets gives the player width rather than a point collision. X and Y are accepted independently so motion can slide along a desk. nearby uses station centres with half-tile offsets.
parts.try: Hold two directions diagonally and compare speed with straight movement. You should not gain a square-root-of-two speed bonus.

parts.title: Claim and cancel work without duplicate owners
parts.why: note keeps a newest-first bounded log. beginJob checks phase, existing work, station state, owner and distance before claiming it. The player job records progress, a puzzle index, deterministic wire sequence and a start time. cancelJob releases the station only if this player still owns it, then clears local work. These ownership checks prevent simultaneous repairs from counting twice.
parts.try: Have two humans press E at the same red station. Only one should claim it; cancel that task and let the other claim it.

parts.title: Complete exactly one job and validate the next step
parts.why: complete clears the fault/owner, increments team and worker counts, restores bounded morale and changes the version before testing victory. jobStep rejects inactive/distant work. Wire tasks compare the next terminal and return early until the final correct input; bug tasks compare one answer; coffee computes elapsed fill from the simulation clock. The client supplies a choice, not a success flag.
parts.try: Choose one wrong wire terminal and confirm no score is awarded. Then repair correctly and check team score increases by exactly one.

parts.title: Resolve failure and deliberately introduce faults
parts.why: A successful step calls complete. A wrong fix costs morale, logs the outcome and releases ownership so work can be retried. prank requires playing state, no current job, no cooldown and a nearby fixed station. It makes a real fault, advances its version, starts a cooldown and costs team morale. This keeps pranks inside the same job/morale model as normal faults.
parts.try: Prank a green station twice rapidly. Only the first should succeed, and its colour should change because broken state changed.

parts.title: Search breadth-first through tile centres
parts.why: The queue starts at the player tile and prev records visited cells plus their parent. Each tile expands four axis neighbours. Because every step has equal cost, the first reached goal gives a shortest tile path. The visited Map prevents loops. Reconstructing parents walks backward, unshift reverses that order, and slice(1) removes the already occupied starting tile.
parts.try: Put a desk on the direct route in a copy. Ada should take a longer walkable path, not move through the desk.

parts.title: Give the AI the same movement and ownership rules
parts.why: The playing guard freezes ended shifts. Each player cooldown decays. Ada either spends time on an owned job or selects the nearest unclaimed fault, uses nearby/beginJob on arrival, and otherwise follows the first BFS waypoint. Human movement uses stored intentions and cancels work when leaving range. The bot’s timed completion is an explicit shortcut for minigames, not a language model.
parts.try: Turn Ada off mid-task and ensure her ownership is released, then turn her back on and observe a real walk to a fault.

parts.title: Create pressure, end the shift and serialize a view
parts.why: This second phase check occurs after player work, so a newly won shift is not immediately subjected to another fault/deadline. nextFault advances on schedule, a fixed station becomes broken, and open faults drain morale by elapsed seconds. Time/morale can lose the shift. publicOffice adds the requesting player ID and copies player/job records into a response shape.
parts.try: Leave several faults unattended and compare morale drain with a nearly clean office. A won shift should stop accumulating new pressure.

nord-office.intro: Connect every HTML control, puzzle panel, canvas layer and polling path to the shared office rules.

parts.title: Declare the page and the available rule operations
parts.why: Imports enumerate the exact local rule functions that the host can invoke. The header/navigation provide solo, shift, AI and pause controls. The canvas size matches 24 by 16 tiles at 32 pixels. The task/result containers separate dynamic interaction from the map so a rendered sprite is not responsible for validating a fix.
parts.try: Find work/cancel controls in the page and later in command(). Trace one control from its ID to the rule call.

parts.title: Collect online details without replacing solo play
parts.why: The sidebar exposes name, room and server plus ticket/log outputs. It explains host ownership and AI behaviour. These are presentation promises implemented later, not a server hidden in the page. After markup, canvas context, held keys and fresh office state are created; the local human and Ada are added explicitly.
parts.try: Choose Solo practice without running Node. The page should still start a complete local shift.

parts.title: Use one command interface for local and online rules
parts.why: request handles timeout, JSON and HTTP errors. command either posts an intention and adopts the returned server state or calls the corresponding shared function locally. The bot branch releases owned work before removing Ada. Clearing taskKey forces the task panel to reflect the new operation. This is where authority changes; rendering code does not need two implementations.
parts.try: Compare a local repair with an online repair. Both should reach jobStep, but only the online one goes through HTTP.

parts.title: Create sessions and keep shared pause honest
parts.why: Solo builds a fresh state and roster. Join adopts the server’s identity and room snapshot only after a successful response. Start and bot use command, while Pause freezes only the local shift. Clearing keys on a join/reset prevents old intent crossing into a new run. Error messages leave the page operable.
parts.try: Join two browsers and click Pause in one. It should explain that the shared shift continues rather than freezing the other player.

parts.title: Find an eligible station and handle keyboard intent
parts.why: work chooses a nearby broken unowned station, then requests a claim. The key handler ignores text inputs, prevents page scrolling and treats E/X/Escape as one-shot actions. Key release/blur clears movement, and blur pauses solo only. Window listeners are paired with teardown at the end.
parts.try: Hold E and verify it does not repeatedly claim/complete a task. Move away from a claimed station and watch it become available again.

parts.title: Rebuild only when the task changes
parts.why: The task key combines identity/progress/puzzle/start time. If unchanged, the UI leaves buttons in place instead of recreating them every frame and losing focus. A small button factory sends step values. Wire labels show the ordered sequence, bug labels show actual faulty JavaScript, coffee adds a fill meter, and Cancel overrides the generic step callback with the cancel route.
parts.try: Click the first correct wire colour. The panel should advance to step two; the score should still be unchanged.

parts.title: Paint tiles and station status
parts.why: The entire canvas is repainted, then map characters choose floor/wall/desk layers. Multiplying tile indices by 32 is the only tile-to-screen conversion. Station markers read broken state for colour and use a sine ring as a visual alert. The ring does not define interaction distance; nearby in rules does.
parts.try: Change the alert ring radius visually. You should still need to stand within the same rule distance to press E.

parts.title: Paint people and derive the HUD
parts.why: Avatars use tile positions converted to pixels, a small shadow, role-dependent clothing, a name and a work indicator. textAlign is restored for later drawing. HUD/result strings read team phase/score/morale/time. No score is awarded here, and a visual success message is not used as a rule condition.
parts.try: Inspect a client snapshot while another intern moves. The same player record should drive both its name and avatar position.

parts.title: Update text only when needed and animate coffee from time
parts.why: Ticket/log text is cached to avoid unnecessary DOM replacement. drawTask decides whether puzzle controls need a rebuild. Coffee’s gradient uses the same elapsed-time formula as validation, while its green target region is fixed. This UI prediction makes the game readable, but the server still determines the result when the pour arrives.
parts.try: Pour just outside the green interval. The animated meter should not grant success merely because the button was clicked.

parts.title: Choose local simulation or online snapshots, then dispose
parts.why: The loop computes clamped seconds and a directional intention from the held-key Set. Solo assigns those axes and calls tickOffice; online sends input, then requests a snapshot, about ten times per second with a busy guard. It never also runs local authoritative rules online. draw remains common. The final getters support inspection; cleanup stops future frames, removes listeners and clears the mount root.
parts.try: Temporarily stop Node and observe the connection message. Rejoin after restarting it; do not expect memory-only rooms to survive a process restart.

nord-office.intro: Implement the complete room API, host controls and stale-input safety.

parts.title: Create a room and add its host
parts.why: The server factory accepts a root/clock/port for both direct use and tests. Join capacity is bounded globally and per room. A new room receives fresh office rules and Ada, then a unique human is added. The first human becomes host, and a session record owns activity/input/action timestamps. Returning publicOffice gives the client its own ID.
parts.try: Join the same room twice with different names. Both should see one room with one Ada, not one bot per browser.

parts.title: Resolve identity and accept only finite axes
parts.why: Subsequent requests locate the session and refresh its activity timestamp. State is read-only output. Input rejects non-number axes, clamps them to a valid range and records when they arrived. Positions are not accepted from the browser. The simulation will use these axes on the server’s tick.
parts.try: Inspect /api/input in the Network panel: it sends dx/dy, not a claimed x/y position or a claimed score.

parts.title: Authorize shared controls and route task intentions
parts.why: Only the host can restart or toggle AI. Removing Ada cancels her task before removing her record. A short action interval bounds repeated work/prank messages. Each endpoint calls the same rule function as solo, then returns a fresh room snapshot. Unknown routes are errors rather than silently succeeding.
parts.try: Try Start from the second human client. It should return a host-only error without resetting the running shift.

parts.title: Stop abandoned movement and release abandoned work
parts.why: Sessions expire after thirty seconds of silence; cleanup cancels owned work and can promote another host. Axes are zeroed much sooner after stale input, preventing walking forever after a lost connection. Empty rooms are deleted; each nonempty room advances once. The static-file allowlist and direct-entry guard finish a server that can also be imported by tests.
parts.try: Close a moving client. It should stop after input expiry, then disappear and release work after session expiry.

nord-office.intro: Read the entire package-free HTTP adapter shared by the game servers.

parts.title: Create an HTTP response boundary
parts.why: The imported Node modules handle sockets, files and paths. serve receives game-specific api/tick callbacks and an explicit public-file map. json writes a content type and disables caching before serializing the result. The origin branch permits same-origin clients and local Nord previews, while rejecting unrelated remote origins. This is a trusted-room development policy, not an account system.
parts.try: Open the game through its Node server, then through Nord Play with the same Server address. Both supported origins should receive JSON.

parts.title: Parse a bounded API message
parts.why: OPTIONS answers a browser preflight before gameplay. API POST bodies must declare JSON, remain under 2048 bytes and parse as an object. GET is allowed for snapshots. Returning early for invalid input prevents malformed messages from reaching game rules. api returns either plain data or a status/data result, which the adapter normalizes through json.
parts.try: Send an invalid action with the browser Network panel and inspect its HTTP status; distinguish transport validation from the game-specific unknown-action error.

parts.title: Serve only named public files and own the tick
parts.why: The file map resolves URL paths to known project files; arbitrary requested disk paths are not joined directly. MIME types tell the browser how to load modules/styles. A catch turns failures into a 500 response. setInterval calls game rules every 50ms, close clears it, and optional port null makes tests control listening. failure and roomCode centralize error shape and safe room naming.
parts.try: Request server.mjs in the browser URL. It should return Not found; the source is distributed through the archive rather than this static allowlist.

nord-office.intro: Read the complete Nord page entry point and its failure path.

parts.title: Load the local runtime and start the app
parts.why: The document declares encoding and viewport, creates the mount container and loads local code. The module imports mount from app.js and awaits initialization for the HTML-tier root. The ready/error flags are inspection signals used by browser checks; they are not a second simulation. The catch logs and exposes initialization errors. The page is served over HTTP so local module and asset URLs resolve consistently.
parts.try: Temporarily rename the imported main module on a copy and reopen Play. Inspect the Console/error path, then restore the correct name.

nord-office.intro: Read every project field that tells Nord which host, display and services to use.

parts.title: Identify the project and choose its presentation
parts.why: format and engineVersion identify the serialized contract, while name/id give human and stable application identity. type chooses the host; startScene is used by a scene backend and is empty for these HTML apps. Display fields request dimensions, fit behaviour, pixel-art treatment and background. Physics selects a runtime engine; the rail shooter uses custom rules with none, while HTML-hosted libraries are initialized in their own modules.
parts.try: Change only the display title/name in a copy and reopen the project. Do not change the stable ID casually if you want to keep the same save namespace.

parts.title: Distinguish scene actions from HTML event handling
parts.why: The input object maps action names to keyboard codes for Nord scene scripts. Vector Patrol reads these through this.input. HTML-tier hosts in the other projects read their own DOM events, so editing this action table alone does not rewrite those handlers. plugins/ui declare ordinary scene services and skin/theme; any remaining desktop configuration is the native capability contract rather than a browser CORS override.
parts.try: For Vector Patrol, add a second fire key and test it. For an HTML app, locate its key handler instead of expecting this table to change DOM input.

nord-office.intro: Read every stylesheet rule, grouped by the UI responsibility it controls.

parts.title: Set the app foundation and reusable visual language
parts.why: The opening rules give html/body a continuous background and minimum height, apply border-box sizing, reset margins and choose system typography. Header, heading and basic control rules establish the app’s hierarchy and affordances. Keeping this local avoids remote font or stylesheet dependencies.
parts.try: Change one accent colour on a copy and reopen Play; no gameplay or saved-document data should change.

parts.title: Place the map next to connection controls
parts.why: The desktop grid assigns the map flexible space and the sidebar a fixed readable column. Canvas scales responsively while retaining its simulation tile units. Buttons/inputs share typography and focusable native controls.
parts.try: Resize the window: the map may scale, but a worker should not gain a different walking speed.

parts.title: Style task feedback and a readable coffee target
parts.why: Pre-line preserves ticket/log line breaks. The task panel contains live buttons, coffee gets a visible bounded meter and the result has stronger colour/size. The narrow-screen rule stacks the sidebar. These are feedback styles, not the logic that awards a repair.
parts.try: Change the coffee border style only. Success must still be decided by the elapsed-time rule, not by CSS colour.

paper-worlds.intro: Build the entire serializable document and common painter before adding either view.

parts.title: Initialize ten independent boards
parts.why: Page dimensions describe drawing coordinates. Array.from produces one board object per ID with a title selected by index. The first page gets text and a sticky, while other pages begin empty. Shape records carry kind, position, colour and text; they do not contain native Phaser/Babylon objects, which would not serialize cleanly.
parts.try: On a fresh save, change one title in this initializer. Existing saved data should still take precedence until you intentionally import/reset it.

parts.title: Seed a door and a graph as ordinary document records
parts.why: These are the remaining properties in the first-page shapes array. The rectangle uses text door as a convention interpreted later by world.js. The pen stores sampled pairs, which both the 2D painter and graph ride can consume. Finishing with an empty array for other boards avoids accidentally sharing the first page’s shapes.
parts.try: Add a pen point to the seed on a fresh copy and observe the same change in the drawing and graph path.

parts.title: Paint the page and the first shape types
parts.why: paint clears its destination before drawing a paper background and dot grid. Every shape resets drawing style so previous colour/line settings do not leak. Pen points become a path; rect uses x/y/width/height and a door gets translucent fill. This painter works with either the Phaser canvas or a Babylon texture context.
parts.try: Disable background only in a temporary painter call and inspect transparency. The stored shapes must remain unchanged.

parts.title: Finish circles, sticky shadows and text
parts.why: A circle interprets w as radius and enforces a small minimum. Sticky shadows are reset immediately after drawing so later text does not inherit blur/offset. Text size depends on kind; splitting and limiting lines prevents a long note from flooding the page. None of these view choices changes the saved note body.
parts.try: Place text after a sticky. Its letters should be crisp instead of inheriting the sticky’s shadow.

parts.title: Treat imported data as a document boundary
parts.why: Validation limits numbers, allowed kinds, colour syntax, text length and point counts. Pen geometry requires finite coordinate pairs; other kinds require position and relevant dimensions. The outer check requires exactly ten titled boards with bounded shape arrays. This prevents malformed imports from reaching drawing methods that expect coordinates.
parts.try: Import a copy with a string where a coordinate should be. It should produce an error and leave the previous document usable.

parts.title: Embed text as inert JSON without changing it
parts.why: JSON.stringify preserves document structure. Escaping less-than characters prevents note text from closing a script data element. Using a replacement callback is equally important: dollar tokens in a replacement string have special meaning to String.replace, while a returned string is inserted literally. This preserves both markup-like text and prices containing dollar signs.
parts.try: Write a note containing <door> and $&. Export the desk and compare the embedded/restored board text with the original.

paper-worlds.intro: Build the complete Phaser drawing interaction and both Arcade minigames.

parts.title: Own view-local state and a Phaser game
parts.why: getBoard supplies the currently selected document without freezing an old array reference. change reports committed edits. The view owns a canvas texture, camera pan/zoom, draft shape and temporary play bodies. Phaser AUTO selects its renderer; Arcade starts with zero global gravity because only bouncing balls need gravity. The fixed internal viewport is separate from the document page size.
parts.try: Switch board selection and verify the next stroke edits the new board, not the board that was selected when the view was created.

parts.title: Create a texture and begin an input transaction
parts.why: The CanvasTexture is displayed at origin zero. Camera bounds allow a wide pannable workspace, and cursor keys serve the maze. Pointer down converts to world coordinates first. Hand mode records initial pan/screen values; text/sticky commit immediately; other tools begin a draft. A draft is not a saved stroke until pointer up.
parts.try: Zoom, place a sticky and compare its position after Fit page. It should stay at its document coordinates.

parts.title: Keep drag geometry separate from committed shapes
parts.why: The draft stores initial coordinates and an initial pen point. The rectangle label is lowercased when interpreting door, so the convention does not depend on letter case. Pointer move computes either camera pan in inverse zoom units or shape geometry. Preview painting appends the draft to a temporary array; it does not keep pushing copies into the document.
parts.try: Drag slowly and inspect shape count before releasing. A long stroke should become one shape, not one saved shape per movement event.

parts.title: Commit once and normalize rectangle directions
parts.why: Pointer up and leaving the game share one completion function. Rectangles dragged left/up get shifted origins and positive dimensions, so collision conversion later can use centres and sizes consistently. Only non-hand drafts enter the document. Clearing drag and repainting removes preview state. Wheel zoom is clamped and reapplied to the camera.
parts.try: Draw the same rectangle down-right and up-left. Both should later create usable maze walls.

parts.title: Move a tiny player and translate coordinates correctly
parts.why: The maze update reads cursor directions, sets velocity and checks the lower-right goal. Reaching it dispatches a host event and destroys temporary play objects. point uses the camera’s world conversion then clamps to the printable page; applyCamera applies zoom and scroll; redraw repaints the current board and refreshes the GPU texture. These helpers centralize transforms and rendering.
parts.try: Pan away from the page, use Fit, then play a maze. Drawing and movement should still agree about page coordinates.

parts.title: Destroy temporary objects before changing modes
parts.why: The player, balls and wall/goal objects belong only to a play session. stopPlay destroys them and clears arrays, leaving document shapes intact. play always calls it first, restores a useful camera framing and sets physics bounds to the entire page. This keeps a second play mode from inheriting the previous mode’s bodies.
parts.try: Start balls, then maze, then Stop. The saved circles/rectangles should remain while moving toys disappear.

parts.title: Turn each circle into a controlled Arcade toy
parts.why: Only circle records become dynamic circles. Radius is bounded for playable size, colour is converted from CSS hex to a Phaser number, and an Arcade body is attached. Bounce, world collision, initial velocity and per-body gravity describe the toy. Registering a collider lets the balls interact with one another; their physical positions are not written back into the document.
parts.try: Draw two circles close together and press Bounce circles. They should collide and move while your original saved circles stay unchanged.

parts.title: Turn rectangles into static walls and add a goal
parts.why: Door rectangles are excluded from walls. The visual rectangle is created from its centre and dimensions, then a static Arcade body is attached. The player gets a circular body/world bounds and a collider with walls. The teal goal is a visual target checked in update. All are registered for Stop cleanup.
parts.try: Draw walls with an open path to the lower-right; then temporarily close that path. The player should be blocked by actual colliders, not merely dark paint.

parts.title: Expose a small view interface after readiness
parts.why: The host waits until Phaser has created the scene before manipulating the view. The returned interface exposes only the operations the host needs, plus the texture canvas for the 3D bridge. Changing tools stops play, Fit changes the camera, and dispose destroys both temporary bodies and the Phaser game. This is explicit ownership across an asynchronous framework startup.
parts.try: Reopen Play after using a minigame. There should be one Phaser canvas and a fresh usable input system.

paper-worlds.intro: Build every 3D representation and interaction from the same saved boards.

parts.title: Lay out ten textured papers
parts.why: createDesk returns the owned Babylon environment. Each board is painted with the common painter after scaling page coordinates to the texture size. Five columns/two rows place the papers; metadata stores the board ID for picking. Paper arrays retain texture and mesh handles for later refresh/focus. Texture content is derived from documents rather than separate 3D-only notes.
parts.try: Edit board zero, enter 3D and click its paper. The editor should return to the same board ID.

parts.title: Translate sticky positions and construct a door
parts.why: Sticky X/Y fractions become offsets across that board’s 3D paper. The box helper adds a physical toy, and metadata marks it as flickable. A door-labelled rectangle causes three glowing frame bars to be built with next-board metadata. The rendered frame is an interpretation of the label, not a direct extrusion of every rectangle.
parts.try: Draw a normal rectangle and one labelled door. Only the labelled one should create a clickable 3D frame.

parts.title: Dispatch picks by metadata
parts.why: Only a completed pick event triggers actions. Sticky picks find their aggregate and apply an impulse at the mesh position. Door picks create a short flight record containing cloned camera targets and destination ID. Plain paper picks select the editor only when no transition/ride owns the camera. This avoids one click starting conflicting actions.
parts.try: Click a sticky and then an empty paper. The first should flick; the second should edit, without treating the desk itself as a board.

parts.title: Animate camera ownership in seconds
parts.why: Door flight interpolates the orbit target over about one second and brings radius inward, then calls select. A graph ride uses a different camera and a sampled path index; it clamps the index so looking at the next point stays valid. At the end, it restores the orbit camera and disposes the temporary camera/tube. These are animations, not edits to board state.
parts.try: Ride the initial graph to its end. Orbit controls should be available again rather than leaving a hidden FreeCamera active.

parts.title: Refresh textures and scatter owned toys
parts.why: Spreading d returns the desk lifecycle along with papers/stickies. refresh clears and uploads the active Phaser canvas into one DynamicTexture; update makes the new pixels visible. shake applies different lateral/upward impulses to each physical note. Neither operation rewrites the saved shape array.
parts.try: Shake notes, return to 2D and compare text/positions. The original document should be intact even though physical poses were chaotic.

parts.title: Convert one stroke into a camera track
parts.why: The last pen stroke with enough points becomes the route. Subsampling limits geometric complexity, coordinate mapping turns page X/Y into track X/Y/Z, and Catmull–Rom creates a smooth sampled curve. A tube displays it. A FreeCamera takes over until the update callback completes the ride. focus is a separate orbit convenience for board selection.
parts.try: Draw a rising/falling graph and ride it. Changing the stroke’s vertical shape should alter camera height, while no rigid-body vehicle is implied.

paper-worlds.intro: Build the entire document host: controls, document selection, async mode changes, persistence, exports and teardown.

parts.title: Create identity and document actions
parts.why: The imports give the host document, views and download operations. The header contains mode/save/export controls and uses the supplied mascot sheet through CSS. These controls are separate from painting so the same document can be acted on in either view. mount owns only the supplied root.
parts.try: Change the subtitle and reopen Play. It should not affect saves or board identity.

parts.title: Declare tools and editing values
parts.why: The sidebar exposes board selection, tool, colour and text. IDs are read later by tool(), so choosing a tool changes data passed into flat.setTool rather than mutating a Phaser object directly from markup. Undo/Fit operate on document or camera respectively; their similar UI placement does not mean they have the same state owner.
parts.try: Follow the color input ID to tool(). Verify the same colour reaches newly drawn shapes, not existing ones.

parts.title: Declare play/backup controls and both surfaces
parts.why: Minigame, shake and ride controls are explicit mode requests. PNG/JSON/import expose recovery tools. The titlebar/badge communicates which representation is active, while only one of the two canvases is visible. The status paragraph is the common error/progress outlet. None of these buttons silently writes files to a disk path.
parts.try: Find the hidden world canvas and the flat container; switch modes and observe visibility changing for the same page.

parts.title: Choose document data before starting Phaser
parts.why: The host reads a versioned save, optionally reads embedded document JSON, validates it and falls back to newBoards. Active index, revision and saved counters are host state. createFlat receives a getter for the current board and a change callback that marks unsaved edits. A captured fixed board object here would break selection/import later.
parts.try: Import a valid JSON backup after editing another board. New strokes should use the imported board array.

parts.title: Wire selections and serialize 3D transitions
parts.why: options rebuilds the selector and title from document data. tool reads current editing values, then Fit sets the opening camera. modeChange chains asynchronous mode requests so rapid clicks cannot create orphaned engines. changeMode creates/replaces the world, refreshes the active texture and pauses Phaser, or hides/stops 3D and resumes Phaser. Errors stay visible in status.
parts.try: Double-click Explore 3D quickly. You should end with one active desk, not multiple render loops.

parts.title: Separate document edits, camera changes and toy actions
parts.why: Board selection changes the getter target and redraws; Undo changes saved shapes/revision; Fit changes only the view. Ball/maze requests return to 2D; Stop removes temporary play state. Shake/ride await a 3D transition before using its world. Maze victory arrives as an event from flat rather than the host guessing coordinates again.
parts.try: Undo once after drawing, then use Fit. Only Undo should change shape count.

parts.title: Save revisions and export simple formats
parts.why: persist writes boards through Nord Save and acknowledges the exact revision only on success. The timer writes only changed documents. PNG reads the drawing canvas into a Blob, while JSON serializes editable records. Their outputs serve different purposes: an image is viewable, a JSON backup can be edited/imported. Storage failure explains the recovery path.
parts.try: Draw, wait for autosave and reload. Then compare a downloaded PNG with a JSON backup: only the JSON contains shape kinds and coordinates.

parts.title: Validate imported files and export a portfolio template
parts.why: Import limits bytes, parses JSON, validates the full document, updates selection/revision, returns to 2D and persists. Export fetches the local template, calls the safe embedding helper and downloads a new HTML page. Missing template and storage errors are reported. The exported HTML still needs the accompanying local modules/vendor folder explained in the guide.
parts.try: Import malformed JSON and confirm the old document remains. Export a valid desk and inspect that it contains all ten boards, not just the active PNG.

parts.title: Offer touch navigation and release the mounted app
parts.why: The initial two-touch distance becomes a comparison baseline; a sufficiently smaller distance requests the same mode function as the button. Passive listeners do not claim to implement every browser gesture. Inspection getters expose current state, and teardown cancels autosave, writes pending edits, disposes both view owners and clears the root.
parts.try: Use the button as the desktop fallback; on supported touch hardware, test the inward pinch. Close/reopen Play and ensure the previous autosave timer does not keep running.

paper-worlds.intro: Build the complete reusable Babylon/Havok desk and browser-download helper.

parts.title: Share pending local script loads
parts.why: The Map caches the promise, not just the presence of a script tag. Rapid callers must all wait until the library is actually ready. onerror removes the failed element/cache entry so a later attempt can retry. This is important because both mode buttons and filter changes can request 3D before the first load finishes.
parts.try: Click the 3D mode button twice rapidly. There should be one ready view, not an undefined BABYLON error.

parts.title: Create one engine, scene and controllable camera
parts.why: createDesk loads the local Babylon file, owns an Engine for the supplied canvas and sets an opaque background. ArcRotateCamera uses alpha/beta/radius around a target; attachControl gives orbit/zoom input. Radius limits avoid entering the paper surface or losing the whole desk at extreme zoom. minZ controls near clipping.
parts.try: Compare orbit dragging with moving a paper: the camera changes the view without altering saved document coordinates.

parts.title: Light a surface and prepare shadow ownership
parts.why: The hemispheric light supplies broad fill; the directional light supplies a direction and shadow map. A restrained specular colour avoids a distracting glossy desk. A solid box, not a zero-thickness drawing, supplies the tabletop. Materials and meshes are scene-owned. The aggregates array will additionally own physics handles that need disposing.
parts.try: Change the directional light direction temporarily and observe where shadows fall, while paper text remains readable.

parts.title: Load the packaged physics binary
parts.why: The local Havok loader receives locateFile so its WASM resolves beside the supplied loader. enablePhysics connects it to this Babylon scene with a gravity vector in 3D units. The tabletop aggregate has mass zero, making it a fixed collider rather than another falling toy. Physics is an optional helper setting, not an editor tier switch.
parts.try: Temporarily set physics false at the helper call. Static papers should still render, but there will be no physical sticky/flick response.

parts.title: Create a writable texture rather than a screenshot file
parts.why: A double-sided plane is laid across the desk. DynamicTexture owns a canvas context that callers can paint, then upload with update. The emissive/unlit material preserves readable colour from either side; zero specular avoids highlights washing out text. The mesh still casts a shadow. The return object exposes mesh, texture and material for later drawing and picking.
parts.try: Draw a bold line in 2D and switch views. It should appear as actual texture content on the corresponding paper.

parts.title: Create a visible rigid sticky toy
parts.why: A small box has physical thickness, a colour material and a shadow caster. A dynamic aggregate supplies mass, restitution and friction. Registering that aggregate gives one disposal owner. The returned mesh supports picking and position inspection; the returned aggregate supports impulses. These are different handles for appearance and physics.
parts.try: Increase restitution slightly and flick a sticky. It should bounce more without changing the original 2D note shape.

parts.title: Own the render loop and resize lifecycle
parts.why: The update Set lets app-specific animations run before scene.render. Delta is converted to seconds and capped for those callbacks. A single resize listener updates the engine. setActive can stop/restart the stored render callback, and dispose releases listeners, aggregates, scene and engine. Replacing a view must call this owner, not merely hide its canvas.
parts.try: Switch back to 2D and observe that the old desk stops animating. Reopening 3D creates one fresh owner.

parts.title: Hand a browser a real downloadable object
parts.why: download accepts a Blob or creates one, creates a temporary object URL and triggers a named anchor download. Revoking shortly afterward releases the temporary URL without invalidating the click immediately. The browser still controls the save destination; this is not an arbitrary filesystem write.
parts.try: Download JSON and verify its suggested filename and contents. Cancel the save if you do not need another copy.

paper-worlds.intro: Understand the complete existing Nord Save helper bundled with this app.

parts.title: Namespace slots and read versioned data
parts.why: The prefix includes the app identity, and slotId chooses one save slot. A private key method keeps naming in one place. Reading returns an empty versioned envelope when missing or invalid, and an optional migration callback upgrades older data. This helper stores serializable values, not engine objects. MemoryStorage is available when no Storage implementation is supplied.
parts.try: Compare the Paper Worlds and RSS River storage prefixes in browser tools. Their saves should not overwrite each other.

parts.title: Read and write values, then define memory storage
parts.why: get supplies a caller default when a value is absent. set reads the envelope, replaces one key, records version/time and serializes through the Storage interface. all/has/delete expose slot operations. MemoryStorage implements the same getItem/setItem/removeItem contract using a Map, which is useful in tests but does not survive page reload. App callers still need to catch storage quota/permission failures on writes.
parts.try: Back up your document, reload the page and verify it returns. Then inspect how the app reports a failed write instead of assuming success.

paper-worlds.intro: Read the entire exported desk template that embeds your documents and opens directly in 3D.

parts.title: Style a standalone viewing surface
parts.why: The page declares UTF-8, viewport and a full-window canvas. Its small header sits above the scene and contains an all-boards action. Styles belong to this standalone page rather than requiring the studio sidebar stylesheet. It is a viewer, so it does not create drawing tools or write the recipient’s saves.
parts.try: Open an exported desk from the served project folder and resize it. The canvas should fill the window and the header should remain reachable.

parts.title: Read embedded data and handle module failures
parts.why: The application/json element is a data container; portfolioHTML replaces its marker safely before download. The module imports the same world code as the editor, parses the embedded boards and focuses a clicked paper. View all restores an overview target/radius. A catch changes hint text if local resources are missing, giving a useful failure rather than a blank unexplained page.
parts.try: Move only the HTML away from its modules on a test copy. Observe the missing-resource failure, then restore the full exported folder.

paper-worlds.intro: Read the complete Nord page entry point and its failure path.

parts.title: Load the local runtime and start the app
parts.why: The document declares encoding and viewport, creates the mount container and loads local code. The module imports mount from app.js and awaits initialization for the HTML-tier root. paper-worlds.intro: Read every project field that tells Nord which host, display and services to use.

parts.title: Identify the project and choose its presentation
parts.why: format and engineVersion identify the serialized contract, while name/id give human and stable application identity. type chooses the host; startScene is used by a scene backend and is empty for these HTML apps. Display fields request dimensions, fit behaviour, pixel-art treatment and background. Physics selects a runtime engine; the rail shooter uses custom rules with none, while HTML-hosted libraries are initialized in their own modules.
parts.try: Change only the display title/name in a copy and reopen the project. Do not change the stable ID casually if you want to keep the same save namespace.

parts.title: Distinguish scene actions from HTML event handling
parts.why: The input object maps action names to keyboard codes for Nord scene scripts. Vector Patrol reads these through this.input. HTML-tier hosts in the other projects read their own DOM events, so editing this action table alone does not rewrite those handlers. plugins/ui declare ordinary scene services and skin/theme; any remaining desktop configuration is the native capability contract rather than a browser CORS override.
parts.try: For Vector Patrol, add a second fire key and test it. For an HTML app, locate its key handler instead of expecting this table to change DOM input.

paper-worlds.intro: Read every stylesheet rule, grouped by the UI responsibility it controls.

parts.title: Set the app foundation and reusable visual language
parts.why: The opening rules give html/body a continuous background and minimum height, apply border-box sizing, reset margins and choose system typography. Header, heading and basic control rules establish the app’s hierarchy and affordances. Keeping this local avoids remote font or stylesheet dependencies.
parts.try: Change one accent colour on a copy and reopen Play; no gameplay or saved-document data should change.

parts.title: Use the supplied sheet and style controls
parts.why: The mascot uses one region of the packaged four-by-two sheet through background size/position. Shared button/input/select/textarea rules keep the studio coherent; labels explain each input and textarea sizing gives notes usable space. Changing sprite position selects a different artwork cell without loading an external image.
parts.try: Temporarily change the sprite background position to another cell, then restore the ghost.

parts.title: Create a studio layout without changing document coordinates
parts.why: The grid assigns sidebar width and flexible workspace. Panels, rules, headings and titlebar communicate editing versus viewing roles. Styling never changes WIDTH/HEIGHT in model.js: browser layout and drawing coordinate systems remain separate.
parts.try: Change sidebar width slightly and verify a saved stroke stays at its document position.

parts.title: Size surfaces, honor hidden state and adapt
parts.why: Both view surfaces share a display area; the inner Phaser canvas scales within it and the 3D canvas disables conflicting browser touch gestures. Status/footer remain legible. The explicit hidden rule wins over display declarations, and the media query reduces sidebar/padding for smaller screens.
parts.try: Switch 2D/3D and verify the inactive surface truly disappears, rather than occupying another blank 640-pixel region.

rss-river.intro: Build all feed configuration, parsing, safe-link and cache-merge logic.

parts.title: Give subscriptions stable identities
parts.why: Each feed has an app ID, display name, endpoint and topic. IDs are used for filtering and article namespacing; labels can change without losing identity. The three sources are defaults, not automatic requests or a bundled current-news database. Fetch is a separate user action so startup can remain offline.
parts.try: Change a source name without changing its ID. Existing cached items should still belong to that source.

parts.title: Normalize links before creating anchors
parts.why: URL resolves relative links against a feed’s address and lets the helper inspect the protocol. Only HTTP/HTTPS survive; malformed input becomes an empty link instead of throwing through the reader. parseFeed then bounds input size and checks XML parser errors and item/entry presence. A successful HTTP response is not enough to prove its body is a feed.
parts.try: Import an HTML error page renamed .xml. It should be rejected rather than shown as fake articles.

parts.title: Extract inert text and choose a usable link
parts.why: The helper parses description markup in an inert document, removes active container elements, then reads normalized textContent. Entry iteration is capped. RSS text links and Atom href links have different forms, so linkNode selects an alternate/default link before safeLink resolves it. Title length is bounded. No publisher HTML is inserted into app controls.
parts.try: Import a description containing bold markup and a script tag. The reader should show text without executing the script or creating a live script element.

parts.title: Choose stable keys and a single article schema
parts.why: The GUID/Atom ID is preferred, then a resolved link, then a title/index fallback. Prefixing with feed.id prevents collisions across sources. All entries become the same fields for title, summary, date, read and star; the UI does not need separate RSS and Atom rendering paths. Summary limits keep the cache practical and the original URL preserves access to the full publisher article.
parts.try: Import one RSS item and one Atom entry. Verify both produce a usable title, plain summary and Read original link.

parts.title: Preserve reading choices while refreshing content
parts.why: A Map indexes old records by stable ID. Each incoming record replaces content but retains previous read/star flags. New IDs become new entries. Converting back to an array and taking the last 240 bounds the small library. This is a deliberate personal cache, not a permanent archive with unlimited history.
parts.try: Star a demo entry, load the demo again, then reload the page. Its star should survive both merging and persistence.

rss-river.intro: Build the complete reader host, filters, both fetch paths, river lifetime and import/backup flow.

parts.title: Create the reading room header and source controls
parts.why: The imports select one schema/merge path, one 3D view owner and existing save/download helpers. Header controls make refresh, native fetch, 3D and backup explicit actions. The sidebar source selector and filters determine a view of cached data, not separate databases. This keeps search usable without networking.
parts.try: Disconnect networking and type in Search after loading the demo. Filtering cached content should still work.

parts.title: Provide separate list, river and reading surfaces
parts.why: The list and river occupy one content area while the article pane remains readable alongside it. Status can report fetch failures without deleting current content. After markup, the host reads saved subscriptions/articles and keeps selected ID and river lifetime separately. Invalid top-level storage values fall back to defaults.
parts.try: Switch list/river and confirm the reading pane does not become a different copy of the article state.

parts.title: Persist carefully and create filter options
parts.why: Persistence writes subscriptions and articles through Nord Save and reports quota errors. feedOptions rebuilds option elements with textContent and preserves a still-valid selection. visible applies source/unread/star/search predicates, then reverses a copy rather than mutating the stored order. Filters compose, so a starred item from another source can still be hidden by source choice.
parts.try: Enable Starred only with no stars. You should see an empty state, not a broken render or an automatic network refresh.

parts.title: Open one article without trusting its markup
parts.why: read finds by ID, marks read and persists. It builds source/title/date/summary nodes using textContent, then wires Star and Flick. Star changes the shared record and may rebuild the river; Flick is temporary visual physics. safeLink controls whether an original anchor is created; noopener/noreferrer isolates the new tab. The final render updates list read styling.
parts.try: Click a story, star it, then search for it. Its title and state should agree between the article pane and list.

parts.title: Rebuild an understandable list from filtered records
parts.why: Each button gets source, title and a bounded summary preview. Classes express read/selected state without changing article content. Empty state tells users how to obtain data. Cached/unread/star counts summarize the whole library, while the heading counts the current filtered list. These are derived values, not counters incremented independently.
parts.try: Mark visible read with a source selected. Other-source unread counts should remain until you read them.

parts.title: Discard superseded asynchronous scenes
parts.why: A version number identifies the newest river request. createRiver can await libraries/physics; if a later filter/mode request wins, this finished scene is disposed instead of taking over the UI. The previous visible river is released only when a current replacement is ready. Mode changes and filters reuse this lifecycle; hiding the river invalidates pending requests.
parts.try: Double-click 3D or change filters rapidly. You should end with the latest view and one live Babylon engine.

parts.title: Fetch intentionally through browser or Nord host
parts.why: Refresh disables the main button and gathers partial failures. The optional bridge is imported only for the native action. Each non-demo source is fetched with an HTTP status check; browser fetch has a timeout and remains subject to CORS, while Nord host fetch goes through declared capabilities. Parsed entries merge into the cache, then the UI is saved/rebuilt. One failed source does not erase successful source results.
parts.try: Refresh while one endpoint is unavailable. Read cached articles afterward and inspect the per-source error text.

parts.title: Wire batch actions and add subscriptions as data
parts.why: The two refresh buttons choose transport explicitly. Mark visible read acts on the current filter. Adding a URL normalizes it, rejects duplicates, creates an identity/name and persists it. Adding a source does not silently grant native host permission, which is why the status explains the manifest requirement.
parts.try: Add the same endpoint twice. The second attempt should report Already subscribed rather than create duplicate source options.

parts.title: Use a real local feed fixture and restore backups
parts.why: demo loads packaged XML through the same parser/merge path as live feeds and clearly names its source as local demo. Import distinguishes a full JSON backup from XML, limits file size, checks required collection/item shapes and rebuilds options/list after success. Imported XML becomes its own named source. Errors go to status.
parts.try: Back up, import that JSON, then import a small XML feed. Verify the first restores state while the second adds a source.

parts.title: Finish startup and release a replaced view
parts.why: Backup serializes both subscriptions and article flags. Initial render happens before the demo fallback, and only an empty cache loads that local fixture. The inspection interface exposes current arrays/view for checks. Teardown marks the host inactive so a pending river request cannot attach later, disposes the view and clears the root.
parts.try: Reload after starring an item. Existing cached data should appear without re-fetching news or replacing it with the demo.

rss-river.intro: Follow every texture, pick, movement, physics and cleanup operation in the 3D reader.

parts.title: Wrap text into bounded canvas lines
parts.why: The view owns a desk and lists of papers/physics bodies. wrapText measures prospective words against available width, paints a line when full and stops at a maximum line count. Line height determines baseline spacing. It works with system fonts and plain strings, avoiding remote page screenshots and publisher images.
parts.try: Use a long title in a demo copy. It should wrap into bounded lines rather than painting across neighbouring paper edges.

parts.title: Paint each article and encode importance spatially
parts.why: Only eighteen visible entries become papers. A star changes width/height, tint and later elevation. The painter reserves separate areas for source, title, summary and status with appropriate fonts/line limits. Metadata stores article ID for the host callback; grid placement prevents opening all papers at the same location. These are views of shared records, not a second article store.
parts.try: Star one story and reopen the river. Its paper should be larger/higher, and clicking it should open that same article ID.

parts.title: Route picks and animate only floating papers
parts.why: A completed pick reads article metadata and calls the same host read function used by list buttons. The update callback moves floating papers slowly, wraps travel at the far edge and uses small sine motions. dropped excludes bodies now owned by physics so animation and Havok do not fight over position.
parts.try: Read one paper from the river, then flick it. Its original read flag remains even after its visual motion changes.

parts.title: Hand one paper over to a rigid body
parts.why: flick ignores missing/already-dropped records, then makes a thin box of matching dimensions. The collider is invisible and receives the old world position; parenting the visual and zeroing its local position preserves appearance. The aggregate adds mass/contact properties, an impulse starts motion, and disposal later releases these aggregates before the desk owner.
parts.try: Press Flick twice on the same story. The second click should not create another body or duplicate the paper.

rss-river.intro: Read the complete original local RSS fixture; it is also an example of the input format.

parts.title: Recognize an RSS channel and stable item IDs

parts.try: Add a ninth item with a new GUID and load the demo again. Existing stars should remain and one new story should appear.

rss-river.intro: Read the entire explicit feed-host allowlist.

parts.title: Distinguish intentional news endpoints from library dependencies
parts.why: These three hostnames declare the app’s deliberate external feed data to Nord’s static URL checker. They do not make browser CORS disappear and do not grant native HTTP capabilities; those are separate boundaries. Babylon, Havok and artwork still load from the project. A new default feed needs an intentional update here and in the appropriate permission configuration.
parts.try: Add a custom source through the UI and compare the stored subscription with this file. They have different responsibilities.

parts.title: Arrange source, list and reading columns
parts.why: The three-column layout gives navigation, a flexible current and a readable article width. Sidebar controls/filter labels and status/count styling distinguish actions from information. Native inputs remain usable; this app does not paint its text fields into 3D.
parts.try: Narrow the window and observe which areas move before changing any article data.

parts.title: Give list entries useful reading states
parts.why: The bounded list scrolls independently. Each story is a full-width button with source, title and excerpt typography. read reduces emphasis while selected restores a clear active border. These classes are a visual projection of article flags, not storage themselves.
parts.try: Read a story and then select another. The first should remain read while the selected border moves.

parts.title: Make article text calm and readable
parts.why: The article pane uses a light paper surface, comfortable line height and a serif title. Source/date/link/button rules retain clear hierarchy. The river canvas has its own bounded area and touch handling so it can be optional. No publisher stylesheet is imported.
parts.try: Open a long summary and inspect line length. The pane should remain useful even when the 3D river is hidden.

parts.title: Adapt columns at two viewport widths
parts.why: The first breakpoint reduces to two columns and places the article below content; the smaller breakpoint stacks the page. The hidden rule ensures list/river mode switching continues to work at either width. Responsive CSS changes presentation, not the subscription cache.
parts.try: Try both breakpoints, then restore a wide window. Your active story and reading flags should still be present.

rss-river.intro: Read the complete bundled Nord bridge used by the optional host-fetch button.

parts.title: Normalize errors and choose request transports
parts.why: The bridge exposes Promise-based operations with stable error codes. Binary helpers convert bytes to/from base64 for transport. IPC assigns request IDs and resolves pending promises when the native host replies; HTTP wraps the same method/params request shape through the local desktop endpoint. RSS River consumes http.fetch but the bridge is shared with other Nord apps.
parts.try: Find where RSS River calls desktop.http.fetch and where this module converts that call into a method/params request.

parts.title: Build bounded browser fallbacks
parts.why: Browser storage is namespaced per app, with an in-memory fallback when localStorage cannot be used. Path normalization rejects external/parent paths for the emulated app-data filesystem. Helpers encode binary files, provide file pickers and snapshot watches. These are browser equivalents of selected desktop features, not unrestricted access to your disk.
parts.try: Run a static browser export and inspect desktop.transport after readiness: it should choose web rather than claim a native host exists.

parts.title: Map supported browser operations explicitly
parts.why: The dispatch table implements app info, local store, virtual files, dialogs, notifications and clipboard using browser APIs and permissions. Files are stored as encoded content; list/stat/watch operate on that virtual namespace. Unsupported methods are rejected after lookup. In particular, this fallback does not grant a browser a universal CORS-bypassing HTTP client.
parts.try: Use Refresh feeds in a plain browser. A blocked publisher still needs XML import or a genuine Nord host, not this fallback.

parts.title: Deliver events and await transport readiness
parts.why: The event Map keeps listener sets, and polling relays host events on the HTTP transport. create chooses native IPC when appropriate, otherwise probes the local host and falls back to web. The internal c function awaits readiness before dispatch, preventing an early click from calling an unselected transport. sub reduces repeated wrapper construction while preserving method names.
parts.try: Call a bridge method just after app startup. It should wait for ready rather than failing because call is still null.

parts.title: Expose capability-shaped wrappers and the shared instance
parts.why: The public object groups file/dialog/notification/clipboard/store/process/network/window/menu operations. Wrappers marshal arguments; real native permissions are enforced by the host. watch returns an unwatch function, and on/off manage callback lifetime. Drag/drop becomes an event. The module finally exports one app-identified instance and exposes it on window.nord.desktop. These APIs do not mean RSS River requests every capability.
parts.try: Compare this API surface with nord.project.json permissions. The reader only declares the feed hosts it needs, not every bridge feature.
